summary: City water-intake crib two miles off 68th Street, built 1892. A temporary crib beside it burned in 1909, killing dozens of men; the light is still listed.

structures.note: Four-sided pyramidal skeletal tower topped by a lantern room (LighthouseFriends); red skeleton tower in the 2025 Light List

structures.name: Edward F. Dunne Crib
structures.note: 110 feet across in 32 feet of water; steel footbridge to the 68th Street Crib

staffing.note: Final crew of keepers withdrawn in 1990 (LighthouseFriends); cribs still in use are staffed remotely (Preservation Chicago)

access.note: Owned by the Chicago Department of Water Management; tower closed; buoyed exclusion zone around each crib.

Security systems installed on all Chicago intake cribs

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends dates the 68th Street Crib to 1892. The 1909 date (and the 15.0 m tower from Wikidata) appears to describe the Edward F. Dunne Crib, 50 feet away, which shares the name 'Dunne Crib' in the record. Human review of the identity before editing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1909 date belongs to the Edward F. Dunne Crib, built 50 feet from the 68th Street Crib. LighthouseFriends dates the 68th Street Crib to 1892.

LighthouseFriends gives 30 January 1909. The Richmond paper (dated 20 January), the Washington Herald and Los Angeles Herald of 21-22 January, and the Tribune's 2020 retrospective all date the fire to 20 January, and the newspapers of 21-22 January already report it. The story uses 20 January.

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story now states LighthouseFriends' 30 January date for the fire alongside the 20 January the papers and the Tribune give; the pumping station is placed five miles inland per LighthouseFriends, with Preservation Chicago's on-shore description noted; the 1866 intake crib is the Two Mile Crib (LighthouseFriends), not this 1892 crib; the 1909 newspaper distances are for the burning Intermediate Crib, not this one. Dynamite quantity (3 tons per workers, 800 pounds per the company) is stated as a disagreement. Melone is named only in his 1964 public role. Death toll unresolved, and the story says so: 25-35 (first wire, Richmond, 20 January); one survivor's estimate of 36 (Richmond); 46 (Washington Herald, 21 January); 47 bodies at the morgue (Los Angeles Herald, 22 January, with a coroner who thought 66 possible and a union president who feared 100); the Tribune's 21 January report of 47 recovered and 48 rescued; the coroner's jury's 60, with estimates to 70 (Tribune 2020); LighthouseFriends' 70 of 100. The Chicago Examiner of 21 January 1909 (67 dead, via Chicagology) could not be read: the Chicagology page came back as binary, so it is not cited. The Mexico Missouri Message of 28 January 1909 (headline '35 are dead') was read but not used; it is a later wire with a count that does not fit the Tribune's. Date: the Richmond header OCR reads 'JANUARY, 30', but the dateline and the Library of Congress issue date (20 January) agree with the Wednesday; LighthouseFriends' 30 January probably follows the header. Crew size: 75 (Richmond), about 80 (Tribune, the usual number), 88 (Washington Herald), 175 (Los Angeles Herald, quoting the union president), 79 names on the company list. Distance: 'about two miles out, opposite Seventy-third street' (Richmond), 'a mile and a half off Seventy-third street' (Washington Herald), about 1.5 miles off 71st Street (Tribune 2020). The story's opening "about two miles" is LighthouseFriends' figure for this crib (map note); the newspaper figures describe the burning Intermediate Crib. The 1893 Light-House Board entry for the 'Emergency Intake Waterworks Crib' (19 October 1892) is not identified with this crib; the story says so. Status: Wikipedia's water-cribs table (lead only; it cites the City of Chicago's 2014 DWM Capital Plan) lists the 68th Street Crib as inactive and the Dunne Crib as active. The City's plan was not read, so the story does not state current use. The 2025 Light List still lists the 68th Street Crib Light. The record's 1909 tower height (15.0 m) and 1909 'built' appear to describe the Dunne structure; the 1892 tower's height is unknown. Keepers: the USLHS archive lists none for this place (roster.py: 'ROSTER: none listed'). The 1964 Tribune article, as LighthouseFriends quotes it, names Robert Melone as in charge of the Dunne crib; he is named only in that public role, and the article's family remarks are left out. The 1909 scenes come from the Richmond, Washington Herald, Los Angeles Herald and Tribune texts, quoted or paraphrased; nothing is added. Preservation Chicago's 2017 demolition plan names the Four Mile and Wilson Avenue cribs, not this one. The Murfin blog (Wikipedia lead) was not read. LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: the story paraphrases it and quotes it sparingly.
